text: A traditional stateful firewall decides what to allow based on connection-level information: address, port, protocol, and whether a connection is established. That tells it that traffic is flowing over port 443, but not what that traffic actually is — two unrelated services can look identical at that level. A next-generation firewall keeps all of that stateful tracking, and adds the ability to look inside the traffic itself to understand what's really passing through.

Deep packet inspection examines the payload, the actual data inside a packet, instead of stopping at the header. Two connections both arriving on port 443 over HTTPS look identical to a traditional firewall. An NGFW running DPI inspects the traffic patterns inside each one and can identify that one is Facebook traffic and the other is a completely different HTTPS service, even though both are encrypted and share the same port.

That ability to tell services apart is application awareness, and an integrated intrusion prevention system builds on it by inspecting traffic for known attack patterns and exploit signatures in real time, blocking malicious traffic even when it looks like a perfectly legitimate, allowed connection. Because the IPS is built into the firewall rather than bolted on separately, it inspects the same traffic DPI already examines, with no second device required.

Application awareness changes what a rule can say. Instead of "block port 443," which would break every HTTPS service on the network, an administrator can write "block Facebook, allow Salesforce" — because the firewall identifies the specific application generating the traffic, not just the port it travels on. Port-based rules are a blunt instrument; application-aware rules let policy follow the actual traffic.

DPI, application awareness, and integrated IPS together are what separate an NGFW from a traditional stateful firewall: the traditional firewall asks whether a connection is allowed, while the NGFW asks what the traffic actually is and whether it's safe.
